questions.q: Read the passage carefully and answer the questions given below: Unemployment has long been one of the most pressing issues in India, but in recent years, a more nuanced problem has come to the forefront — skill mismatch. While millions of Indians are actively seeking jobs, industries often struggle to find workers with the right skills. This paradox highlights a deep disconnect between the education system, vocational training programs, and the actual demands of the job market. India is home to one of the largest youth populations in the world, with more than 65% of its citizens under the age of 35. This demographic advantage, often referred to as the ‘demographic dividend,’ holds enormous potential. However, if not harnessed through proper education, training, and employment opportunities, it risks becoming a demographic disaster. The real issue lies not just in unemployment, but in ‘educated unemployment’ — where even degree holders remain jobless due to irrelevant or outdated skills. According to multiple reports, including those by NITI Aayog and the India Skills Report, employers across sectors such as manufacturing, IT, healthcare, and construction frequently cite a shortage of employable talent. Graduates often lack practical exposure, problem-solving ability, communication skills, and technical expertise — competencies that are vital in today’s dynamic job environment. This mismatch stems largely from a theoretical, exam-driven education system that prioritizes rote learning over real-world application. Furthermore, while India produces over a million engineering graduates annually, a large percentage of them remain underemployed or unemployed. On the other hand, sectors such as renewable energy, AI, cybersecurity, healthcare, and data science are facing talent shortages due to lack of trained professionals. The problem is exacerbated in rural and semi-urban areas, where access to quality training and digital infrastructure is still limited. Government initiatives like Skill India, PMKVY (Pradhan Mantri Kaushal Vikas Yojana), and National Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme (NAPS)have attempted to bridge this gap. However, the outcomes have been mixed due to poor implementation, lack of industry collaboration, and low awareness among youth. There is a pressing need to align these schemes more closely with market demand, involve private sector players in curriculum development, and promote vocational education and lifelong learning as viable alternatives to traditional degrees. Additionally, reskilling and upskilling the existing workforce is crucial in a time of rapid technological advancement. The rise of automation and artificial intelligence threatens to make many jobs obsolete while creating demand for new roles that require entirely different skill sets. In conclusion, tackling unemployment in India requires a shift in focus from merely creating more jobs to creating the right kind of jobs and equipping people with the right kind of skills. Bridging the gap between education and employability is not just an economic necessity, but a social imperative. Only by addressing the root causes of skill mismatch can India fully capitalize on its demographic advantage and ensure inclusive, sustainable growth. Answer the following questions;

questions.q: Read the following passage and answer the questions that follow: Peer pressure is a phenomenon wherein we tend to get influenced by the lifestyle and the way of thinking of our peers. Peer pressure can prove beneficial but it is most often observed to have negative effects. The thought, behaviour and taste in fashion, music, television and other walks of life of the masses are often seen to have a deep impact on society. We tend to get influenced by the lifestyle of our peer group. The changing way of life of our peers often force us to change our ways of looking at life and leading it. It is a human tendency to do what the crowd does. Few have the courage to resist the peer pressure and be their own selves. Peer pressure is bound to affect most of us both positively and negatively. The distinction between positive and negative peer pressure lies in a thoughtful analysis of the views of the masses. Following your peers blindly leaves a negative impact on your life while an analytical approach of looking at peer behaviour can help you act positively. Peer pressure is not always bad. It can help you analyse yourself and contemplate on your ways of life. Some of the practices that the masses follow may actually teach you the way of living. You may be able to change yourself for the better. Looking at what others do, can help you bring about a positive change in your way of thinking. If you can pick selectively, peer pressure can actually result in a positive change in your way of life. Teens are in that phase of life when you are exposed to the world outside. These are the years when you spend most of your time with your friends. Teens is the phase of beginning to become independent in life, the years of forming your ideals and principles, the years that shape your personality and the years that introduce you to your own self. As adolescents, you often spend most of your daily time with friends and owing to this, you tend to imitate your friends. The people around you are bound to influence you. Parents and teachers need to be careful while dealing with teenagers, as they are most susceptible to succumbing to peer pressure during these years of their life. Teenage individuals need to be taught to distinguish between the good and the bad, the right and the wrong and should be taught to be thoughtful in life. A strong support from family, an ability to differentiate between positive and negative and the skill to choose friends from among the peers- this pronged strategy is the best way to keep away from negative peer pressure.
